extracted.intended_audience: USPTO examiners, patent prosecutors, patent attorneys, and applicants
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on construing claim language (transitional phrases, contingent clauses, printed matter, machine-readable media) and applying those constructions for novelty/obviousness and eligibility determinations under the MPEP.

rubrics_metrics.name: "consisting essentially of" transitional phrase
rubrics_metrics.description: The transitional phrase “consisting essentially of” limits the scope of a claim to the specified materials or steps “and those that do not materially affect the basic and novel characteristic(s)” of the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use case law (In re Herz, PPG Industries v. Guardian Industries, Atlas Powder, In re Janakirama-Rao, Water Technologies v. Calco) to interpret. It occupies a middle ground between “consisting of” (closed) and “comprising” (open). For purposes of searching/applying prior art under 35 U.S.C. 102 and 103, absent a clear indication in the specification or claims of what the basic and novel characteristics are, “consisting essentially of” will be construed as equivalent to “comprising.” Applicants bear the burden of showing that additional steps or materials in the prior art are excluded by “consisting essentially of” language (In re De Lajarte). Specification statements defining what materially changes the invention (e.g., AK Steel specifying silicon content ≤ 0.5% and deleterious effects above that level) can provide basis to limit scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transitional phrases generally (e.g., "having", "composed of")
rubrics_metrics.description: Transitional phrases such as “having” must be interpreted in light of the specification to determine whether open or closed claim language is intended.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation depends on facts and the specification. Example: Lampi Corp. interpreted “having” as open terminology; Crystal Semiconductor noted “having” does not create a presumption that the claim body is open; Regents v. Eli Lilly shows ‘having’ can permit inclusion of other moieties in context. The phrase “composed of” has been interpreted like “consisting of” or “consisting essentially of” depending on the facts and specification (AFG Industries, In re Bertsch). Always read the transitional phrase with the specification and other evidence to decide scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: "adapted to", "adapted for", "wherein", "whereby" clauses
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim scope is not limited by claim language that suggests or makes optional but does not require steps to be performed, or by claim language that does not limit a claim to a particular structure. Examples of language that may raise limiting-effect questions include: (A) “adapted to” or “adapted for” clauses; (B) “wherein” clauses; and (C) “whereby” clauses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether such clauses are limitations depends on case-specific facts. Use case law: Griffin v. Bertina (wherein clause limited process claim because it gave meaning/purpose to manipulative steps); In re Giannelli (an “adapted to” clause limited a machine claim where written description made clear a narrower meaning); Hoffer v. Microsoft (a “whereby” clause stating a condition material to patentability cannot be ignored). But courts may decline to give weight to a “whereby” clause that merely expresses an intended result of a positively recited process step (quoting Minton v. NASD). Read clauses in context of the specification and claim as a whole.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contingent limitations — broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI) differences for method vs system claims
rubrics_metrics.description: The broadest reasonable interpretation of a method (process) claim having contingent limitations requires only those steps that must be performed and does not include steps that are not required because the condition(s) precedent are not met. The broadest reasonable interpretation of a system (apparatus/product) claim having structure that performs a function which only needs to occur if a condition precedent is met requires structure for performing the function should the condition occur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the distinction illustrated in Ex parte Schulhauser (PTAB Apr. 28, 2016). For a method claim, if a claimed invention may be practiced without a condition occurring, then the contingent step is not required under BRI. For a system claim, the claimed structure must be present regardless of whether the condition occurs. Consequence: Examiner need not present obviousness evidence for method steps not required under BRI, but to render a system claim obvious the prior art must teach the structure that performs the contingent function along with other limitations. See also MPEP § 2143.03 for contingent claim limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Printed matter analysis — threshold: is the limitation directed to printed matter?
rubrics_metrics.description: A limitation is printed matter only if it claims the content of information. The first step of printed matter analysis is determining that the limitation in question is in fact directed toward printed matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use In re DiStefano and related cases to determine whether the limitation claims content (printed matter). If not directed to printed matter, do not proceed to printed-matter-specific inquiry. If it is printed matter, proceed to determine functional/structural relationship to substrate. Note that printed matter analysis has been extended to method claims where instructional limitations are added to a known method (assess whether a new and nonobvious functional relationship exists).

rubrics_metrics.name: Printed matter — functional relationship requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Once it is determined that the limitation is directed to printed matter, the examiner must determine if the matter is functionally or structurally related to the associated physical substrate; only if the answer is 'no' is the printed matter owed no patentable weight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A functional relationship exists where the printed matter performs some function with respect to the product (e.g., indicia on a measuring cup indicating volume) or where the product performs some function with respect to the printed matter (e.g., hatband arranging numbers to satisfy an algorithm). Cite Lowry, Gulack, In re Miller. If no functional relationship exists (product just a support for conveying a message to a human reader), printed matter is not given patentable weight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence against functional relationship (printed matter)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a product merely serves as a support for printed matter, or the claim as a whole is directed toward conveying a message or meaning to a human reader independent of the supporting product, no functional relationship exists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include images on a hatband not arranged in sequence, a deck of cards with pictures (functions relate to game-play rather than structure), a measuring tape with wiring information unrelated to the tape's structure, or a kit with generic instructions not tied to that specific set of chemicals. See Gulack, In re Bryan, Ex parte Gwinn. Where printed matter and product do not depend upon each other, printed matter lacks functional relationship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functional relationship must be new and nonobvious
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if a functional relationship between printed matter and product is found, the relationship must be new and nonobvious to be given patentable weight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After finding a functional relationship, investigate novelty and nonobviousness using prior art; a color-coded indicia that functions to indicate expiration date could be a functional relationship but still be anticipated or obvious in view of prior art or combinations of prior art. Apply standard novelty/obviousness analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Machine-readable media — printed matter and functional relationship considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: When determining the scope of a claim directed to a computer-readable medium containing certain programming, the examiner should look to the relationship between the programming and the intended computer system. Where the programming performs some function with respect to the computer, a functional relationship will be found. Where the claim as a whole is directed to conveying a message or meaning to a human reader independent of the intended computer system, and/or the medium merely serves as a support for information or data, no functional relationship exists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: A medium programmed with attribute data objects that facilitate retrieval/addition/removal of information establishes a functional relationship (citing Lowry). A memory stick storing batting averages or musical tracks merely supports information and is not functionally related to the computer. Additionally, a claim to a computer-readable medium storing instructions or executable code that recites an abstract idea must be evaluated for eligibility under 35 U.S.C. 101 (see MPEP § 2106).
